heading: Food insecurity in families with autistic children and young people
text: Food insecurity occurs when a household does not have stable access to sufficient, appropriate and nutritious food. This review examined the literature on food insecurity in families with autistic children and young people.
The meta-analysis of nine studies calculated an approximate pooled prevalence of **29%**. After an adjustment related to publication bias, the estimate was around **31%**.

However, this figure needs to be interpreted very cautiously. Heterogeneity between studies was extraordinarily high, above 99%. This means that results differed greatly between studies and that there is no single figure that can simply be applied to every family with an autistic child.

The review also found that food insecurity worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic in some studies and that it could be related to greater caregiver stress and additional difficulties with eating patterns.

The authors emphasise that policies addressing food insecurity should not be limited to financial support alone. In households with autistic people, specific sensory, nutritional and behavioural needs may also be relevant.
The literature suggests that food insecurity is an important problem for some families with autistic children and young people.

It is not correct to turn this result into the statement that 'one in three autistic families experiences food insecurity'. The very high heterogeneity and possible publication bias prevent the percentage from being interpreted as a universal prevalence figure.
notProven: It is not correct to turn 29–31% into a universal prevalence figure for autistic families in every country.
linea: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies, with 9 included in the meta-analysis. It is not correct to turn 29–31% into a universal prevalence figure for autistic families in every country.

heading: Executive function and emotional regulation in autism, ADHD and co-occurrence
text: Executive function includes processes such as planning, inhibition, working memory, cognitive flexibility and behavioural control. Emotional regulation refers to the processes through which a person identifies, modulates and responds to emotional states.
The review examined how these two dimensions relate to one another in autism, ADHD and co-occurring autism and ADHD.

Of the 22 articles included, **16 studied ADHD, 4 studied autism and only 2 studied co-occurring autism and ADHD**. This distribution matters because it shows that much of what is known comes from ADHD research and that evidence specific to co-occurrence remains limited.

Overall, the studies supported an association between greater executive difficulties and greater emotional dysregulation in the conditions examined. However, the magnitude and form of this relationship varied according to participant age and the type of measure used. Results were not identical when executive functions were assessed with performance tasks and when questionnaires or reports of everyday behaviour were used.
Executive function and emotional regulation appear to be meaningfully related in autism and ADHD and may be useful transdiagnostic dimensions for research.
With only two studies focused on co-occurrence, the review cannot define a specific or distinctive 'AuDHD' profile or determine with confidence how it differs from autism or ADHD on their own.
notProven: It cannot define a specific AuDHD profile or reliably distinguish co-occurrence from autism or ADHD on their own.
linea: Systematic review of 22 articles. It cannot define a specific AuDHD profile or reliably distinguish co-occurrence from autism or ADHD on their own.

heading: Belonging and not belonging among transgender and gender-diverse autistic adults
authors: Katie Munday, Steven K. Kapp and Charlotte Morris
text: The study explored how transgender and gender-diverse autistic adults experience belonging and exclusion across different areas of their lives. The researchers used narrative interviews and reflexive thematic analysis.

The findings were organised across different levels. In employment, participants described difficulties accessing suitable jobs, obtaining adjustments and remaining in environments that could be socially or sensorily difficult. Some people turned to self-employment or frequent job changes to gain more control over their environment.

In education, communities and social spaces, some people found places where they could feel understood, especially in certain autistic or queer communities. However, these spaces were not automatically accessible either: sensory, social or other barriers could still be present.

In healthcare, participants described **gatekeeping**, lack of professional knowledge, costs, bureaucracy and experiences of ableism or transphobia. Some participants felt that being autistic negatively affected how professionals interpreted their decisions relating to gender identity.
At the closest interpersonal level, chosen families, supportive relationships and certain forms of communal living appeared as important sources of recognition and belonging.
Belonging does not depend only on individual identity. It is shaped by employment, education and healthcare structures, by the accessibility of spaces and by interpersonal relationships.
With 13 participants, the study cannot calculate frequencies or represent every experience of transgender and gender-diverse autistic people.
notProven: With 13 participants, it cannot calculate frequencies or represent every experience.
linea: Qualitative study with 13 transgender and gender-diverse autistic adults. With 13 participants, it cannot calculate frequencies or represent every experience.

heading: Autistic burnout
authors: Dorota Ali, Mackenzie Bougoure et al.
text: The review synthesised qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods research on how autistic people describe and experience what is known as **autistic burnout**.

Across the reviewed studies, an experience of intense exhaustion repeatedly appeared alongside a reduction in the ability to carry out activities that had previously been possible. For some people it could last for long periods and alternate with episodes of more acute crisis.

Factors associated with burnout included sensory and social overload, sustained masking, stigma, lack of adjustments, the demands of everyday life and difficulty identifying or communicating internal states.
Reported consequences included poorer wellbeing, reduced participation in community activities, difficulty maintaining responsibilities and lower positive expectations about the future.

Factors related to recovery or protection included greater understanding of one's own needs, access to support, rest, time alone and sensory relief. The authors note, however, that individual coping strategies alone do not solve the problem when environmental demands remain incompatible with the person's needs.

The review also highlights an important limitation: most participants in the available literature were white adults, women, diagnosed later in life and with at least average verbal or intellectual abilities.

There is a growing and relatively consistent research base describing autistic burnout as a disabling experience of exhaustion and reduced capacity associated with sustained demands and poorly adjusted environments.
'Autistic burnout' remains a research concept and is not, by itself, an established diagnosis in the main diagnostic manuals.
notProven: Autistic burnout remains a research concept and is not, by itself, an established diagnosis in the main diagnostic manuals.
linea: Systematic review with thematic synthesis covering 48 studies and approximately 4,000 autistic people. Autistic burnout remains a research concept and is not, by itself, an established diagnosis in the main diagnostic manuals.

heading: Healthcare access for young people with intellectual disability
text: This review examined how children and adolescents with intellectual disability use healthcare services and what factors hinder or facilitate access to care.
The included studies examined hospital admissions, emergency services, mental-health care and other healthcare resources.

Compared with young people without intellectual disability, young people with intellectual disability generally had more hospital admissions, more emergency-department visits, longer hospital stays, greater use of some outpatient mental-health services, more 30-day readmissions and more care-related complications. Some studies also reported higher mortality.
Factors that facilitated access included having healthcare coverage and using visual supports or other tools adapted to the person's communication and understanding.
Barriers included lower socioeconomic status, communication difficulties with professionals and limited knowledge about intellectual disability among healthcare providers.

The review notes that findings came from very different healthcare systems, including Australia, the United States, England and other countries, so the barriers are not necessarily identical in every setting.
The evidence shows important inequalities in healthcare use and outcomes for young people with intellectual disability.
The review does not identify a single intervention that resolves these inequalities and does not support assuming that every barrier is present in every country or healthcare system.
notProven: It does not identify a single intervention that resolves these inequalities, and the healthcare systems studied were very different.
linea: Systematic review of 33 studies. It does not identify a single intervention that resolves these inequalities, and the healthcare systems studied were very different.

heading: Behavioural interventions in FASD
text: The study brought together reviews of non-pharmacological interventions for children and adolescents with FASD.
Positive signals appeared in executive functions, social problem-solving and emotional regulation, among other areas.
notProven: Overall quality was uneven: only two reviews were high quality, two were low quality and three were critically low quality according to AMSTAR-2.
linea: Review of systematic reviews covering 7 systematic reviews. Overall quality was uneven: only two reviews were high quality, two were low quality and three were critically low quality according to AMSTAR-2.

heading: Autism, gender diversity, health and healthcare
sample: 1,094 cisgender autistic adults + 174 transgender/gender-diverse autistic adults + 1,295 cisgender non-autistic adults
authors: Kate Green, Elizabeth Weir, Lily Wright, Carrie Allison and Simon Baron-Cohen
text: The study compared health and healthcare experiences across three groups of adults: cisgender autistic people, transgender or gender-diverse autistic people, and cisgender non-autistic people.
Both autistic groups reported more health problems and considerably poorer healthcare experiences than the non-autistic group.

Compared with the cisgender non-autistic group, transgender or gender-diverse autistic people were 2.3 times more likely to report a physical-health condition, 10.9 times more likely to report a mental-health condition and 5.8 times more likely to report self-harm.

Differences in healthcare experience were very broad. Both autistic groups reported poorer experiences on 50 of the 51 items assessed, including communication with professionals, healthcare-related anxiety, access, ability to advocate for one's own needs, healthcare-system problems, sensory experiences and situations involving shutdowns or meltdowns.

When the two autistic groups were compared directly, transgender or gender-diverse participants had even poorer outcomes on a smaller set of indicators related to communication, access, advocacy and shutdowns.
The research documents important healthcare inequalities for autistic people and points to additional risks for some transgender or gender-diverse autistic people.

The study is cross-sectional and based on self-report. The sample was not representative of the whole population and overrepresented white people, UK residents, people with university education and people assigned female at birth.
notProven: It is cross-sectional and based on self-report; the sample did not represent the whole population and was skewed on several demographic characteristics.
linea: Cross-sectional survey study with 1,094 cisgender autistic adults + 174 transgender/gender-diverse autistic adults + 1,295 cisgender non-autistic adults. It is cross-sectional and based on self-report; the sample did not represent the whole population and was skewed on several demographic characteristics.

heading: ARFID prevalence and methodological quality
authors: Rebecca Nicholls-Clow, Melanie Simmonds-Buckley and Glenn Waller
text: The study estimated ARFID prevalence and examined how much the estimate changes when methodological quality is taken into account.
The conventional estimate was 11.14%, but it fell to 4.51% when study quality was weighted. Heterogeneity was close to 99.6%.
notProven: It is not rigorous to present either 11.14% or 4.51% as the universal prevalence of ARFID.
linea: Preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 studies and 122,861 participants. It is not rigorous to present either 11.14% or 4.51% as the universal prevalence of ARFID.

heading: Family–school partnership in selective mutism
design: Qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis
authors: R. Adamson, L. Powell and M. Chilokoa
text: The study explored how families and teachers experience the collaboration needed to support children and young people with selective mutism.

Selective mutism means that a person can speak in some settings but is unable to do so in others. In school this can create substantial difficulties and may be misunderstood if it is treated simply as shyness, opposition or unwillingness.

The researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with four parents and three teachers. Experiences reported by families were predominantly negative, while teachers more often described positive experiences.

Despite this difference, the analysis identified shared elements that supported useful collaboration: **actively listening to families, involving them in decisions, recognising their knowledge of the child, sharing priorities and building mutual trust**.
The authors also highlight the need for schools to understand selective mutism better and to have specific training so they can work effectively with families.
The study provides qualitative information about the features families and teachers value in a good collaborative relationship.
The sample included only seven participants and came from a limited context. It cannot establish universal recommendations or measure which strategy produces better outcomes.
notProven: The sample included only seven participants and cannot support universal recommendations or estimate the effectiveness of strategies.
linea: Qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis with 4 parents + 3 teachers. The sample included only seven participants and cannot support universal recommendations or estimate the effectiveness of strategies.

heading: European guidelines on psychological interventions for tics and Tourette syndrome
design: European clinical guideline based on evidence review
sample: Review of clinical evidence available up to 2021
text: These guidelines review the available evidence on psychological interventions for Tourette syndrome and other tic disorders.

**Psychoeducation** is considered an important first step. It means providing clear and understandable information about tics, their course, management options, treatments and their impact on everyday life. On its own, it is not the intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing tic severity, but it can improve knowledge and attitudes among family members, teachers and peers.

The largest body of experimental evidence was found for **habit reversal training (HRT)** and, in particular, the expanded **CBIT —Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics—** programme. HRT teaches a person to recognise the tic and sensations that may precede it and to use a response that is incompatible with performing the tic.

There is also evidence for **exposure with response prevention (ERP)**. In this approach, the person practises tolerating premonitory sensations and delaying or resisting tics for progressively longer periods. The evidence base is smaller than for HRT/CBIT because fewer studies are available.

The guidelines indicate that when psychoeducation is not sufficient and intervention is considered necessary, HRT/CBIT and ERP can be considered first-line psychological treatments. Access to trained professionals remains an important limitation.
Among psychological interventions for tics, the strongest evidence is for HRT/CBIT. ERP also has scientific support, although from a smaller evidence base.

Not every tic requires treatment. The decision depends on the impact on the person, their functioning and their preferences. The guidelines also do not imply that an intervention produces the same result for every person.
1. Autistic unmasking: authenticity and lower masking burden, but social risks and substantial individual variability.
2. GGOC-AD: small to moderate short-term effects on OCD-related beliefs and symptoms; no general effect on anxiety, depression or self-esteem.
3. Sleep and anxiety: poor sleep quality is consistently related to adolescent anxiety; trials add further evidence.
4. Adult ADHD diagnosis: it can be validating and help people reinterpret their own lives, but it can also involve grief, stigma and difficulty accessing support.
notProven: Not every tic requires treatment, and a guideline does not imply that an intervention will produce the same result for everyone.
linea: European clinical guideline based on a review of clinical evidence available up to 2021. Not every tic requires treatment, and a guideline does not imply that an intervention will produce the same result for everyone.
